title: Creating Your First Project
description: Learn how to use the .NET CLI to scaffold a new ASP.NET Core MVC project, understand the project template options, and run your first application locally.

blocks.text: The **.NET CLI** (Command Line Interface) is your primary tool for creating, building, and running ASP.NET Core projects. It is cross-platform, scriptable, and the same tool that Visual Studio uses behind the scenes. Learning the CLI commands gives you a solid foundation that works everywhere.
In this lesson, you will use the `dotnet new` command to create your first MVC project and `dotnet run` to launch it in a browser.

The `dotnet new` command creates a new project from a template. A template is a pre-configured set of files and folders designed for a specific type of application. For this course, you will primarily use the **MVC template**, which sets up controllers, views, models, and static files for a complete web application.

blocks.title: Creating a new MVC project
blocks.content: Use the .NET CLI to create a new ASP.NET Core MVC project named MyFirstApp.
blocks.code:
dotnet new mvc -n MyFirstApp
cd MyFirstApp

blocks.text: The `-n` flag sets the project name to `MyFirstApp`. The command creates a new folder with that name containing all the files and folders your project needs. The `cd` command navigates into the new project directory.

Once inside your project folder, run `dotnet run` to compile and launch the application. The first run will take a little longer as the SDK restores NuGet packages and builds the project from scratch.

blocks.title: Running the project
blocks.content: Build and run the ASP.NET Core MVC project. Open the displayed URL in a browser.

blocks.text: When the application starts, the terminal displays the URLs it is listening on, typically `http://localhost:5000` and `https://localhost:5001`. Copy the HTTPS URL into your browser to see the default ASP.NET Core welcome page.

blocks.title: Hot reload
blocks.text: .NET 6+ includes hot reload, which lets you change C# or Razor files while the app is running and see the changes immediately without restarting. After saving a file, the terminal shows a hot reload notification, and the browser updates automatically.
The .NET SDK ships with many built-in templates. Run `dotnet new --list` to see all of them. Here are the most relevant ones for web development:

blocks.title: Common web-related templates
items: **mvc** — Full MVC project with Controllers, Views, Models, and static files
**webapi** — REST API project optimized for JSON endpoints with Swagger support
**razor** — Razor Pages application with page-focused routing
**blazorserver** — Interactive server-side Blazor application using C#
**web** — Minimal API project with a single Program.cs file

blocks.title: Choosing the right template
blocks.text: For this course, use the **mvc** template. If you want to build an API without HTML pages later, use the **webapi** template. You can always add more features to any project later.
When you run `dotnet new mvc`, the CLI creates a folder structure with several important files. Let us look at what each part does:

terms.definition: The entry point of the application where the web host is configured, middleware is added, and the app is launched.
A configuration file for storing settings like connection strings, API keys, and application options in JSON format.
The folder for static files such as CSS stylesheets, JavaScript files, images, and fonts that are served directly to browsers.
C# classes that handle incoming HTTP requests and return responses. Each controller typically manages a related set of actions.
Razor (.cshtml) files that generate HTML responses. Views use C# code embedded in HTML to render dynamic content.

blocks.text: To stop the running application, press `Ctrl+C` in the terminal. Any changes you make to C# files while the app is stopped will be picked up the next time you run `dotnet run`. If you have hot reload enabled (automatic in .NET 6+), you can keep the app running and see code changes reflected without restarting.

items.text: A new MVC project folder has been created
items.hint: The folder name should match the `-n` value passed to `dotnet new mvc`
Run `dotnet build` and confirm no error messages appear
Run `dotnet run` and open the HTTPS URL shown in the terminal

items.text: The default ASP.NET Core page is visible in the browser
items.hint: Look for the blue ASP.NET Core welcome page with navigation links
Change a string in Program.cs or a view, save, and confirm the browser updates

blocks.title: Create and Run Your First MVC Project
blocks.description: Create a new ASP.NET Core MVC project from scratch, run it, and confirm it works in your browser.
steps: Open a terminal and create a new folder called `MyFirstApp` for your workspace
Run `dotnet new mvc -n MyFirstApp` to scaffold the project
Navigate into the new project folder: `cd MyFirstApp`
Run `dotnet build` and confirm it succeeds with no errors
Run `dotnet run` and copy the HTTPS URL from the terminal
Paste the URL into a browser and confirm the default ASP.NET Core welcome page loads
blocks.expectedOutcome: A browser window showing the ASP.NET Core welcome page with links for Home, Privacy, and other pages. The terminal should show the app is listening on ports 5000 and 5001.

blocks.title: Lesson Summary
points: The `dotnet new mvc` command scaffolds a complete MVC project with controllers, views, and static files
`dotnet run` builds and launches the application, showing the listening URLs in the terminal
Multiple project templates exist (mvc, webapi, razor, blazorserver, etc.) for different app types
Hot reload lets you see code changes instantly without restarting the server
The first run restores NuGet packages and takes slightly longer than subsequent runs
blocks.takeaway: Creating an ASP.NET Core project is a single CLI command away. The real work begins after the project is scaffolded, as you customize controllers, views, and models to build your application.
